scenes.visual: Title card: Pressure and the Clock.

scenes.tts: Stay up all night. Near dawn, you can barely keep your eyes open.
scenes.visual: A clock face sweeps through the night. A sleepiness meter beside it climbs and peaks near dawn; a figure at a desk slumps.
scenes.narration: Stay up all night. Near dawn, you can barely keep your eyes open.

scenes.tts: By early afternoon, still without sleep, you feel better. How can more time awake make you less sleepy?
scenes.visual: The clock face sweeps on to early afternoon; the meter eases down. On-screen question: More time awake, less sleepy?
scenes.narration: By early afternoon, still without sleep, you feel better. How can more time awake make you less sleepy?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: If time awake were all that mattered, the afternoon would feel worse. Something else changed: a clock.
scenes.visual: Two bars labelled hours awake: the afternoon bar is taller than the dawn bar. A question mark resolves into a small clock icon.
scenes.narration: If time awake were all that mattered, the afternoon would feel worse. Something else changed: a clock.

scenes.tts: The first process is sleep pressure. It builds while you are awake, quickly at first, then more slowly. While you sleep, it drains.
scenes.visual: Axes appear: time of day along the bottom, sleep pressure up the side. A curve labelled Process S rises steeply, bends toward a dashed ceiling, then falls during a night band, faster than it rose.
scenes.narration: The first process is sleep pressure. It builds while you are awake, quickly at first, then more slowly. While you sleep, it drains.

scenes.tts: The second process is a clock in your brain. It keeps a cycle of about a day, even with no windows.
scenes.visual: A windowless room with a person inside; a small clock icon in the brain ticks. Label: Process C: circadian clock, about 24 h.
scenes.narration: The second process is a clock in your brain. It keeps a cycle of about a day, even with no windows.

scenes.tts: The clock's main push is toward waking. It is hardest in the late afternoon and evening, weakest in the early morning.
scenes.visual: An arrow from the clock icon labelled circadian wake drive. A gentle wave across a day peaks over late afternoon and evening and dips over early morning.
scenes.narration: The clock's main push is toward waking. It is hardest in the late afternoon and evening, weakest in the early morning.

scenes.tts: Put both on one graph. An upper wavy line is the level pressure must reach before you fall asleep.
scenes.visual: Back on the axes, an upper wavy line is drawn above the rising pressure curve. Label: upper level, fall asleep here.
scenes.narration: Put both on one graph. An upper wavy line is the level pressure must reach before you fall asleep.

scenes.tts: A lower wavy line is the level it must drain to before you wake. Both lines rise and fall with the clock.
scenes.visual: A lower wavy line is drawn. The pressure curve animates over two days: up to the upper line (moon icon), down to the lower line (sun icon), a sawtooth.
scenes.narration: A lower wavy line is the level it must drain to before you wake. Both lines rise and fall with the clock.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea, in the simple model of an adult's undisturbed sleep. Sleep pressure climbs while you are awake and drains while you sleep.
scenes.visual: A boxed card: The one idea. First sentence appears.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea, in the simple model of an adult's undisturbed sleep. Sleep pressure climbs while you are awake and drains while you sleep.

scenes.tts: You fall asleep when it climbs to an upper level. You wake when it drains to a lower one. The clock raises both levels by day and lowers them by night.
scenes.visual: The rest of the card fills in, matching the lesson's box word for word.
scenes.narration: You fall asleep when it climbs to an upper level. You wake when it drains to a lower one. The clock raises both levels by day and lowers them by night.

scenes.tts: Why two levels? Replace them with one line midway between, and the model chatters on and off at that line. The gap keeps this model's sleep in one long block.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: a single wavy line midway between the two levels; the pressure curve chatters along it and a sleep-wake bar strobes. Small label: illustration of possible numerical chattering, single midway line. Right: two lines with a gap; the bar is one solid night.
scenes.narration: Why two levels? Replace them with one line midway between, and the model chatters on and off at that line. The gap keeps this model's sleep in one long block.

scenes.tts: Back to the all-nighter. Staying up means refusing sleep after pressure crosses the upper level. Near dawn, the clock has pulled that level low. So pressure sits far above it, and you feel very sleepy.
scenes.visual: The graph shows enforced waking: no night band, and pressure keeps climbing past the upper line. At dawn, a tall bracket between pressure and the upper line, labelled excess: illustrative sleepiness proxy.
scenes.narration: Back to the all-nighter. Staying up means refusing sleep after pressure crosses the upper level. Near dawn, the clock has pulled that level low. So pressure sits far above it, and you feel very sleepy.

scenes.tts: By early afternoon, pressure is higher still. But the clock has lifted the level, so the excess has shrunk.
scenes.visual: At early afternoon, the upper line has risen and the bracket, still labelled excess: illustrative sleepiness proxy, is much shorter.
scenes.narration: By early afternoon, pressure is higher still. But the clock has lifted the level, so the excess has shrunk.

scenes.tts: When you finally sleep, will you get back every hour you lost?
scenes.visual: On-screen question: Every lost hour back?
scenes.narration: When you finally sleep, will you get back every hour you lost?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: No. Recovery sleep is longer than usual, but nowhere near hour for hour. Much of the payback comes as deeper sleep.
scenes.visual: A long bar of lost hours beside a much shorter bar of extra sleep. The extra-sleep bar is shaded darker, labelled deeper slow-wave sleep.
scenes.narration: No. Recovery sleep is longer than usual, but nowhere near hour for hour. Much of the payback comes as deeper sleep.

scenes.tts: Can the two processes be pulled apart? In rats, destroy the clock: the supra-kye-az-matic nucleus, just above the optic chiasm.
scenes.visual: A rat brain from below; a small paired nucleus above the optic chiasm glows, labelled suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), then is removed.
scenes.narration: Can the two processes be pulled apart? In rats, destroy the clock: the suprachiasmatic nucleus, just above the optic chiasm.
scenes.caption: Can the two processes be pulled apart? In rats, destroy the clock: the suprachiasmatic nucleus, just above the optic chiasm.

scenes.tts: Sleep scatters across day and night. Yet after a spell without sleep, these rats still slept more, and more deeply.
scenes.visual: A day-night bar fills with scattered sleep blocks in light and dark. Then a keep-awake period and a large, darker block of sleep. Label: pressure still repaid.
scenes.narration: Sleep scatters across day and night. Yet after a spell without sleep, these rats still slept more, and more deeply.

scenes.tts: Keep this. Pressure climbs and drains, and the clock sets the levels.
scenes.visual: The two-process graph returns, clean: sawtooth pressure between two wavy lines. Takeaway card.
scenes.narration: Keep this. Pressure climbs and drains, and the clock sets the levels.
